name: Rajma
steps: Soak the rajma overnight, or in hot water for two hours if you are cooking today.
Pressure cook the rajma with the turmeric and a little salt until it presses soft between two fingers. Keep the cooking water.
Heat the oil and crackle the cumin. Add the onion and cook until it turns pale gold.
Add the ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook down until the oil separates at the edges.
Stir in the red chilli powder and garam masala, then tip in the rajma with its water.
Simmer for fifteen minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot to thicken the gravy.
Finish with the coriander and serve with rice.

name: Chole
steps: Soak the chana overnight, then pressure cook with turmeric and salt until soft.
Brown the onion in oil over a medium flame — properly dark at the edges, not just translucent.
Add ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the masala looks thick and glossy.
Stir in the coriander powder and garam masala, then add the chana with a cup of its water.
Simmer fifteen minutes, mashing a few chickpeas to thicken it.
Finish with coriander and a squeeze of lemon if you have one.

name: Dal Tadka
steps: Rinse the dal and boil it with turmeric and salt until it collapses — about fifteen minutes in a pressure cooker.
Whisk the cooked dal so it turns creamy, adding hot water until it pours like thick cream.
Heat the oil in a small pan. Add cumin, asafoetida and the onion and fry until golden.
Add the garlic and tomato and cook until the tomato breaks down.
Pour the tadka over the dal, add the red chilli powder off the heat, and stir once.
Scatter coriander and serve with rice or roti.

name: Dal Makhani
steps: Soak the urad dal and rajma together overnight.
Pressure cook them with turmeric and salt until completely soft, then mash lightly.
Cook the onion, ginger and garlic in oil until soft, add the tomatoes and cook until pulpy.
Add the mashed dal, half the butter and a cup of hot water.
Simmer on the lowest flame for twenty minutes, stirring now and then so it does not catch.
Stir in the garam masala, red chilli powder and the rest of the butter just before serving.

name: Palak Paneer
steps: Wash the spinach well. Blanch it in boiling water for two minutes, then drop it into cold water so it keeps its colour.
Squeeze out the water and blend to a smooth purée.
Fry the onion in oil until soft, add the ginger and garlic, then the tomato if using.
Pour in the spinach purée and cook gently for five minutes — do not let it boil hard or it darkens.
Fold in the paneer cubes and simmer two minutes so they soak up the gravy.
Season with garam masala and salt, and serve with roti.

name: Paneer Butter Masala
steps: Simmer the tomatoes with the onion, ginger and garlic until they are completely soft.
Blend and pass through a sieve for a smooth gravy.
Melt the butter, add the red chilli powder off the heat so it does not burn, then pour in the gravy.
Cook it down for ten minutes until it deepens in colour and thickens.
Add the milk, sugar, garam masala and salt, then slide in the paneer cubes.
Simmer gently for five minutes and serve with rice or naan.

name: Aloo Gobhi
steps: Cut the potatoes into wedges and the cauliflower into florets about the same size.
Heat the oil and add the cumin, then the onion if using, and fry until soft.
Add the potatoes and cook for five minutes, turning so they pick up colour.
Add the cauliflower, turmeric, coriander powder and salt, and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on a low flame for twelve minutes, shaking the pan rather than stirring so the florets stay whole.
Uncover, raise the heat for two minutes to dry off any moisture, and finish with coriander.

name: Bhindi Masala
steps: Wash the bhindi and dry it completely — any water left on it will make it slimy.
Top and tail each one and cut into two or three pieces.
Fry the bhindi in the oil on a fairly high flame until the stickiness is gone and the edges are browned. Take it out.
In the same pan, add the cumin and onion and cook until golden.
Return the bhindi with the turmeric, coriander powder, red chilli powder and salt.
Toss for three or four minutes, add coriander, and serve with roti.

name: Jeera Rice
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then soak it for ten minutes and drain.
Heat the oil and fry the cumin until it darkens and smells nutty.
Add the onion if using and cook until soft and golden.
Add the drained rice and toss for a minute so every grain is coated.
Pour in the water, add salt, and bring to a boil. Cover and cook on the lowest flame for twelve minutes.
Rest off the heat for five minutes, then fork through gently.

name: Vegetable Pulao
steps: Soak the rice for fifteen minutes and drain well.
Cut the carrot and beans into small pieces, roughly the size of the peas.
Fry the cumin in oil, then the onion until golden.
Add the vegetables and cook for three minutes so they lose their raw edge.
Add the rice, salt and water. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook low for twelve minutes.
Rest for five minutes before opening, then fluff with a fork.

name: Moong Dal Khichdi
steps: Rinse the rice and moong dal together and soak for fifteen minutes.
Heat the oil, add the cumin and asafoetida, then the onion if using and cook until soft.
Add the carrot and the drained rice and dal, and stir for two minutes.
Add the turmeric, salt and water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for eighteen minutes, until the dal has broken down and the rice is soft.
Rest for five minutes. It should be loose enough to eat with a spoon, so add hot water if it tightens.

name: Egg Bhurji
steps: Beat the eggs with the turmeric and salt until no streaks of white remain.
Fry the onion in oil until soft and lightly golden.
Add the tomato and green chilli and cook until the tomato collapses.
Pour in the eggs and let them set for twenty seconds before you start stirring.
Scramble over a low flame until just set — take it off while it still looks a little glossy.
Finish with coriander and eat with pav or roti.

name: Masala Omelette
steps: Chop the onion, tomato, chilli and coriander as finely as you can.
Beat them into the eggs with the salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a flat pan until a drop of egg sizzles on contact.
Pour in the egg and tilt the pan to spread it thin.
Cook for two minutes until the edges lift, then fold in half.
Slide onto a plate and eat straight away.

name: Egg Curry
steps: Boil the eggs, cool them in water, peel and halve them.
Fry the onion in oil until deep golden — this is where the gravy gets its sweetness.
Add the ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the oil separates.
Stir in the coriander powder, turmeric and garam masala, then add a cup of water and simmer ten minutes.
Slide in the egg halves cut side up and simmer for three minutes so they heat through.
Finish with coriander and serve with rice.

name: Home-style Chicken Curry
steps: Rub the chicken with turmeric and salt and leave it while you prepare the masala.
Brown the onions slowly in the oil — give them ten minutes, not three.
Add the ginger and garlic, then the tomatoes, and cook until the mixture is thick and dark.
Add the chicken and turn it in the masala until every piece is coated.
Cover and cook for twenty minutes on a low flame, stirring twice. The chicken will release enough water of its own.
Uncover, add the garam masala and cook off the excess liquid until the gravy clings to the pieces.
Finish with coriander.

name: Butter Chicken
steps: Marinate the chicken in the curd with a pinch of the red chilli powder and salt for at least half an hour.
Sear the chicken in oil in batches until browned but not cooked through. Set aside.
Simmer the tomatoes with the onion, ginger and garlic until completely soft, then blend and sieve.
Melt the butter and cook the purée down for fifteen minutes until it turns a deep orange.
Return the chicken with half a cup of hot water and simmer for ten minutes.
Add the garam masala, sugar and salt, taste, and adjust with a little more butter if it is sharp.

name: Tandoori Chicken
steps: Slash the chicken pieces a couple of times so the marinade gets inside.
Mix the curd, lemon juice, ginger, garlic, red chilli powder, garam masala and salt into a thick paste.
Coat the chicken completely and leave it in the fridge for at least two hours, overnight if you can.
Heat the oven to 220°C, or get a heavy pan very hot.
Cook for twenty-five minutes, turning once and brushing with the oil, until the edges char in places.
Rest for five minutes before serving with onion rings and lemon.

name: Chicken Pulao
steps: Soak the rice for twenty minutes and drain.
Brown the onions in the oil until deep golden and set half aside for later.
Add the ginger, garlic and chicken and fry until the chicken loses its pink colour.
Stir in the curd, turmeric and garam masala and cook for five minutes.
Add the rice, salt and water. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook low for fifteen minutes.
Rest for ten minutes, then fork through and top with the reserved onions.

name: Sambar
steps: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric and salt until soft, then mash it smooth.
Soak the tamarind in half a cup of hot water and squeeze out the pulp.
Boil the onion, tomato and carrot in a cup of water until just tender.
Add the tamarind water, sambar powder and the mashed dal, and simmer for ten minutes.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the asafoetida and pour it in.
Simmer two more minutes and serve with rice or idli.

name: Tomato Rasam
steps: Cook the toor dal with turmeric until soft and mash it.
Crush the black pepper and cumin roughly with the back of a spoon.
Simmer the tomatoes and tamarind pulp in two cups of water for eight minutes, then mash the tomato into the liquid.
Add the dal, the crushed spices, garlic and salt. Bring just to the point of boiling, then take it off — boiling hard kills the aroma.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds with the curry leaves and pour it over.
Scatter coriander and drink it from a cup, or serve with rice.

name: Rava Upma
steps: Dry roast the rava in a pan until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker. Tip it onto a plate.
In the same pan, heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds and add the onion, chilli and curry leaves.
Add the carrot and fry for two minutes.
Pour in the water with the salt and bring it to a rolling boil.
Tip in the rava in a steady stream while stirring, so no lumps form.
Cover and cook for three minutes, then squeeze over the lemon and fluff with a fork.

name: Ven Pongal
steps: Dry roast the moong dal until it smells warm and turns pale gold.
Rinse it with the rice and pressure cook both with the water and salt until very soft — three whistles.
Mash the mixture while it is still hot so it turns creamy.
Heat the ghee and fry the pepper, cumin, ginger and curry leaves for a minute.
Pour the ghee and spices over the pongal and stir through.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or just on its own.

name: Cabbage Poriyal
steps: Shred the cabbage finely — the finer it is, the faster it cooks.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds and add the curry leaves and chilli.
Add the cabbage, turmeric and salt and toss over a high flame for three minutes.
Cover and cook for four minutes. It should keep a little bite.
Uncover, add the coconut and toss for another minute until the raw smell goes.
Serve as a side with rice and sambar.

name: Lemon Rice
steps: Cook the rice so the grains stay separate, then spread it on a plate to cool.
Heat the oil and fry the peanuts until they are a shade darker, then set them aside.
In the same oil, pop the mustard seeds and add the curry leaves, chilli and turmeric.
Take the pan off the heat and squeeze in the lemon juice — adding it off the flame keeps it from turning bitter.
Tip in the cooled rice and salt and fold gently until the colour is even.
Top with the peanuts and serve at room temperature.

name: Curd Rice
steps: Cook the rice until quite soft, then let it cool a little — hot rice will split the curd.
Mash the rice roughly with the back of a spoon and stir in the curd and salt.
Add a splash of water if it looks stiff; it should be loose enough to spoon.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds with the curry leaves and ginger, and pour it over.
Stir through and finish with coriander.
Serve cool, with pickle on the side.

name: Peanut Chutney
steps: Dry roast the peanuts on a low flame until the skins loosen and they smell toasted. Rub off the skins.
Cool them completely — grinding warm peanuts gives a pasty chutney.
Grind with the chilli, coconut, tamarind, garlic and salt, adding water a spoon at a time.
Stop at a coarse, spoonable texture rather than a smooth paste.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds and pour over the top.
Serve with idli, dosa or as a sandwich spread.

name: Aloo Posto
steps: Soak the posto in a little water for ten minutes, then grind to a thick paste with one green chilli.
Cut the potatoes into small cubes — about the size of a pea, so they cook quickly.
Heat the oil, add the mustard seeds, then the potatoes and turmeric, and fry for four minutes.
Add the posto paste and salt and stir for a minute so it coats every piece.
Add a few tablespoons of water, cover, and cook on a low flame for eight minutes until the potatoes are done.
Finish with a slit green chilli and a drizzle of raw mustard oil if you have it. Serve with rice.

name: Bengali Masoor Dal
steps: Rinse the masoor dal — it cooks in fifteen minutes and needs no soaking.
Boil it with turmeric and salt until it falls apart, skimming off the foam at the start.
Heat the oil, add the cumin, then the onion and fry until soft and sweet.
Add the tomato and cook until it melts into the oil.
Pour the dal in, add the red chilli powder and simmer for five minutes.
Finish with coriander and a squeeze of lemon.

name: Shorshe Maach
steps: Rub the fish with turmeric and salt and leave it for ten minutes.
Soak the mustard seeds in water for half an hour, then grind with one green chilli and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste. Keep the paste thick.
Fry the fish lightly in the oil, a minute on each side, and lift it out. Do not cook it through.
In the same oil, cook the mustard paste gently for two minutes — it should not brown or it turns bitter.
Add a cup of water and bring to a simmer, then slide the fish back in.
Cover and cook for six minutes on a low flame, then serve with rice.

name: Bengali Khichuri
steps: Roast the rice and dal together in a dry pan for three minutes until they smell warm.
Fry the cumin in the oil, then add the potato and cauliflower and brown them lightly.
Add the roasted rice and dal and stir for two minutes.
Add turmeric, salt and the water and bring to a boil.
Cook covered on a low flame for twenty minutes, stirring occasionally so it does not catch.
Add the peas five minutes before the end. It should be loose and porridge-like — serve with a fried egg or pickle.

name: Besan Dhokla
steps: Whisk the besan with water, lemon juice, turmeric, sugar and salt into a batter with no lumps — it should pour like thick cream.
Rest it for ten minutes while you heat water in a steamer.
Stir a teaspoon of baking soda into the batter at the last moment and pour it into a greased tin.
Steam for eighteen minutes. A skewer should come out clean.
Cool for five minutes, then cut into squares.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds with the chilli, add a splash of water and spoon it over the dhokla. Scatter coriander.

name: Gujarati Kadhi
steps: Whisk the curd with the besan and a cup of water until completely smooth — any lumps will stay lumpy.
Add the ginger, chilli, turmeric, sugar and salt.
Cook on a low flame, stirring constantly, for twelve minutes. It thickens as it heats; never let it boil hard or it splits.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the curry leaves and pour into the kadhi.
Simmer two more minutes, then scatter coriander.
Serve over rice with a spoonful of ghee on top.

name: Methi-free Thepla
steps: Grate the carrot and mix it with the atta, curd, spices, salt and a tablespoon of the oil.
Add water a little at a time and knead into a firm dough — firmer than chapati dough.
Rest it for ten minutes, then divide into small balls.
Roll each one thin, dusting with dry flour so it does not stick.
Cook on a hot tawa for a minute, flip, brush with oil, and press until brown spots appear on both sides.
Stack them under a cloth so they stay soft. They keep for a day in a box, which is the point.

name: Sev Tameta
steps: Chop the tomatoes roughly — no need to be neat, they break down anyway.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the onion if using and fry until soft.
Add the tomatoes, turmeric, sugar and salt and cook for ten minutes until they collapse into a loose gravy.
Mash lightly with the back of the spoon and add a splash of water if it is too thick.
Take it off the heat and only then scatter the sev on top, so it stays crisp.
Finish with coriander and serve with rotli.

name: Masala Pasta
steps: Boil the pasta in well-salted water until just short of done, and keep a cup of the cooking water.
Soften the onion and garlic in the oil, then add the capsicum and cook two minutes.
Add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a sauce — about eight minutes.
Season with salt and plenty of black pepper, and loosen with the pasta water.
Tip in the pasta and toss over the heat for a minute so it absorbs the sauce.
Grate the cheese over the top if you have it.

name: Chickpea Salad
steps: If you are using dried chana, soak and boil them until tender and let them cool. Tinned ones just need draining and rinsing.
Dice the onion, tomato and cucumber small and even.
Whisk the lemon juice with the oil, salt and pepper.
Toss everything together and leave it for five minutes so the chickpeas take on the dressing.
Taste and add more lemon or salt — salads like this need more than you expect.
Scatter coriander and eat as it is, or spoon it into a roti.

name: Shakshuka
steps: Cook the onion in the oil until soft, then add the garlic, cumin and capsicum.
Add the tomatoes with the salt and cook for twelve minutes until the sauce is thick and jammy rather than watery.
Make small wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon.
Crack an egg into each well and season the tops with pepper.
Cover the pan and cook on the lowest flame for six minutes — the whites should set while the yolks stay loose.
Scatter coriander and bring the pan to the table with bread.

name: Tomato Soup
steps: Roughly chop the tomatoes and onion — no precision needed, it all gets blended.
Soften the onion and garlic in the oil without colouring them.
Add the tomatoes, sugar and salt and cook for fifteen minutes until they have completely collapsed.
Add two cups of water and simmer for five minutes.
Blend until smooth, then pass through a sieve if you want it silky.
Season with pepper, and float a piece of toasted bread on top if you have it.

name: Vegetable Fried Rice
steps: This is best with rice cooked the day before and kept in the fridge — fresh rice steams instead of frying.
Dice the vegetables small and keep them all the same size.
Get the pan properly hot, add the oil and the garlic, and stir for ten seconds.
Add the vegetables and stir-fry for three minutes. They should still squeak when you bite them.
Add the rice, breaking up any clumps with your fingers as you go.
Splash the soy sauce around the rim of the pan, season with pepper, and toss for two minutes before serving.

name: Garlic Mushroom Toast
steps: Wipe the mushrooms clean rather than washing them, and slice them thickly.
Get a dry pan very hot and add the mushrooms with no fat at all — let them squeak and brown for three minutes.
Only then add the butter and garlic. Doing it in this order stops them going soggy.
Season with salt and plenty of pepper and cook two more minutes.
Toast the bread until it is crisp enough to hold up.
Spoon the mushrooms over the toast, with all the butter from the pan, and finish with coriander.

name: Poha
steps: Put the poha in a colander and rinse it under running water for thirty seconds, then leave it to drain. It softens in its own steam — do not soak it.
Fry the peanuts in the oil and set them aside.
Pop the mustard seeds, add the onion and chilli and fry until the onion is soft.
Add the turmeric and salt, then the drained poha, and fold gently. Stirring hard will mash it.
Cover for two minutes on a low flame to heat through.
Squeeze over the lemon, add the peanuts and coriander, and serve.

name: Besan Chilla
steps: Whisk the besan with the water, turmeric and salt until it is smooth and pours easily.
Stir in the finely chopped onion, tomato, chilli and coriander.
Rest the batter for ten minutes so the besan hydrates — it makes a softer chilla.
Spread a thin film of oil on a hot tawa and pour a ladleful of batter, spreading it outwards with the back of the ladle.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge and cook for two minutes, then flip and cook one more.
Stack them as you go and serve with curd or pickle.

name: Aloo Paratha
steps: Knead the atta with water and a pinch of salt into a soft, pliable dough. Rest it for fifteen minutes.
Boil and mash the potatoes while still warm, then mix in the cumin, chilli, coriander and salt. The filling must be dry — wet filling tears the paratha.
Divide the dough and filling into equal portions, filling slightly smaller than the dough ball.
Flatten a dough ball, put the filling in the centre, gather the edges up and seal, then roll out gently.
Cook on a hot tawa for a minute, flip, spread ghee on the cooked side, flip again and press until it puffs and browns.
Serve hot with curd and pickle.

name: Cucumber Raita
steps: Whisk the curd until it is smooth and pourable, adding a spoonful of water if it is thick.
Grate the cucumber and squeeze out the water in your fist — this is what stops the raita going thin.
Fold the cucumber through the curd.
Toast the cumin briefly in a dry pan and crush it, then stir it in with the salt.
Finish with coriander and chill until you serve it.

name: Paneer Bhurji
steps: Crumble the paneer with your fingers into rough, uneven pieces — grated paneer goes gluey.
Fry the cumin and onion in the oil until the onion is soft and golden.
Add the tomato and chilli and cook until the tomato is completely soft.
Add turmeric and salt, then the paneer, and toss for two minutes only.
Take it off the heat while it still looks a little loose; it firms up fast.
Finish with coriander and serve with roti.

name: Clear Chicken Soup
steps: Put the chicken, onion, garlic and carrot in a pot with the cold water. Starting cold is what gives a clear broth.
Bring it slowly to a simmer and skim off the grey foam that rises — do not let it boil hard or it turns cloudy.
Simmer gently for twenty minutes, then lift out the chicken and shred it, discarding the bones.
Strain the broth and return it to the pot with the shredded chicken and sliced carrot.
Season generously with pepper and salt, and simmer five more minutes.
Finish with coriander and serve with bread.

name: Vegetable Sandwich
steps: Slice the tomato and cucumber thinly and pat them dry with a cloth — wet slices make the bread soggy.
Butter every slice right to the edges; the butter is what keeps the bread from going soft.
Layer the vegetables, season with salt and pepper, and close the sandwich.
Press it lightly with your palm so it holds together.
Cut in half on the diagonal, which somehow makes it taste better.
Eat within the hour.

name: Baingan Bharta
steps: Rub the brinjals with a little oil and roast them directly over a flame, turning, until the skin blisters all over and the flesh collapses. About fifteen minutes.
Put them in a bowl and cover for five minutes — the steam loosens the skin.
Peel off the charred skin and mash the flesh roughly. Do not blend it; it should keep some texture.
Fry the cumin, garlic and onion in the oil until golden.
Add the tomatoes, turmeric and salt and cook until the tomatoes are jammy.
Stir in the mashed brinjal and cook for five minutes, then finish with coriander.

name: Lauki Sabzi
steps: Peel the lauki and cut it into cubes about an inch across. Discard the seedy core if it is spongy.
Heat the oil, add the cumin, then the lauki and fry for three minutes.
Add the turmeric, coriander powder and salt and toss to coat.
Add the tomato if using, cover, and cook on a low flame for twelve minutes. Lauki releases plenty of water, so add none.
Uncover and cook off any excess liquid until the pieces look glazed.
Finish with coriander and serve with roti.

name: Egg Fried Rice
steps: Use cold cooked rice, broken up with your fingers so there are no clumps.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt.
Heat half the oil until it shimmers, pour in the eggs and scramble them fast, then take them out while still soft.
Add the rest of the oil and stir-fry the onion, carrot and peas for three minutes.
Add the rice and toss over a high flame for two minutes, then return the eggs.
Season with soy sauce and pepper and serve straight from the pan.

name: Dal Fry
steps: Boil the dal with turmeric and salt until soft, then mash it lightly and loosen with hot water.
Fry the cumin and onion in oil until the onion is golden at the edges.
Add the ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the tomato collapses.
Stir in the red chilli powder, then pour the dal in and simmer for five minutes.
Finish with garam masala and serve with rice.

name: Panchmel Dal
steps: Rinse all the dals together and soak for twenty minutes — the chana dal needs the head start.
Pressure cook them with turmeric and salt until they hold their shape but squash easily.
Fry cumin and asafoetida in oil, then the onion until soft, then the tomato.
Pour in the cooked dals with their water and simmer for ten minutes.
Stir in the garam masala and serve with rice or roti.

name: Lobia Curry
steps: Soak the lobia overnight, then boil it with turmeric and salt until tender.
Brown the onion properly — this curry is bland if you rush it.
Add ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the oil separates.
Add the coriander powder, then the lobia with a cup of its water.
Simmer fifteen minutes, finish with garam masala, and serve with rice.

name: Chana Palak
steps: Boil the soaked chana until soft and keep a cup of the water.
Blanch the spinach for two minutes, drain and chop roughly — no need to purée it.
Fry cumin, garlic and onion in oil until the onion is soft.
Add the tomato if using, then the spinach, and cook for three minutes.
Add the chana with its water, season with turmeric and salt, and simmer ten minutes.
Finish with garam masala and serve with roti.

name: Aloo Matar
steps: Cut the potatoes into small cubes so they cook in the same time as the peas.
Fry cumin in oil, then the onion if using, until soft.
Add the potatoes and fry for three minutes so they take on colour.
Add turmeric, coriander powder and salt, then a cup of water, and cover for eight minutes.
Add the peas and cook uncovered for five minutes until the water thickens.
Mash one or two potato cubes against the pan to thicken the gravy.

name: Matar Paneer
steps: Simmer the tomatoes with the onion and ginger until soft, then blend to a smooth gravy.
Heat the oil, add cumin, then pour in the gravy — it will spit, so stand back.
Cook the gravy down for eight minutes until it darkens.
Add the peas with half a cup of water and cook for five minutes.
Slide in the paneer cubes, add salt and garam masala, and simmer three minutes only.
Serve with roti or rice.

name: Shahi Paneer
steps: Soak the cashews in warm water for twenty minutes, then grind them to a paste.
Boil the onion, tomato and cardamom together until soft, then blend and sieve.
Cook the purée in the oil for ten minutes until it thickens and turns glossy.
Stir in the cashew paste and cook five more minutes — it catches easily, so keep moving.
Add the cream, sugar, red chilli powder and salt.
Fold in the paneer, warm through for three minutes, and finish with garam masala.

name: Paneer Tikka
steps: Cut the paneer into thick cubes — thin slices dry out on the heat.
Whisk the curd with the red chilli powder, garam masala, salt and a squeeze of lemon.
Coat the paneer, capsicum and onion in the marinade and leave for twenty minutes.
Thread onto skewers or spread on a tray and brush with oil.
Grill at 220°C or cook in a hot pan for eight minutes, turning once.
Dust with chaat masala and serve with lemon.

name: Malai Kofta
steps: Boil and mash the potatoes, then mix with crumbled paneer, salt and the cornflour.
Roll into small balls. If the mix is sticky, add another spoon of cornflour.
Fry the balls in medium oil until golden, then drain on paper.
Make a gravy by simmering onion and tomato until soft, blending and straining it.
Cook the gravy down for ten minutes, then stir in the cream and garam masala.
Add the koftas only when you are ready to serve — they soften if they sit.

name: Gobhi Paratha
steps: Knead the atta with water and a pinch of salt into a soft dough and rest it fifteen minutes.
Grate the cauliflower and squeeze out the water in your fist — this is what stops the paratha tearing.
Mix the cauliflower with cumin, chilli, coriander and salt.
Stuff a dough ball, seal the edges, and roll out gently with a light hand.
Cook on a hot tawa, brushing with ghee, until brown spots appear on both sides.
Serve hot with curd.

name: Mooli Paratha
steps: Grate the radish and squeeze it hard — radish holds a lot of water and will ruin the dough.
Mix the dry grated radish with ajwain, chilli and salt.
Knead a soft atta dough and rest it for fifteen minutes.
Stuff, seal and roll each paratha out without pressing too hard.
Cook on a hot tawa with ghee until golden on both sides.
Eat straight away with butter and pickle.

name: Missi Roti
steps: Mix the atta and besan with the spices, salt and chopped onion.
Add water gradually and knead into a firm dough — softer than this and it sticks to the tawa.
Rest for ten minutes, then divide and roll into discs about the thickness of a coin.
Cook on a hot tawa, turning twice, and brush with ghee at the end.
Stack under a cloth and serve with curd.

name: Bajra Roti
steps: Mix the bajra flour with salt and add hot water a little at a time — hot water makes it pliable.
Knead for a few minutes until it stops cracking.
Shape into balls and pat out with your palm rather than a rolling pin.
Cook on a hot tawa for two minutes a side, pressing the edges down with a cloth.
Finish over a direct flame for twenty seconds a side so it puffs.
Serve with ghee and jaggery, or with any sabzi.

name: Vegetable Kofta Curry
steps: Boil the potatoes, mash them and mix with grated paneer, cornflour and salt.
Roll into balls and shallow fry until evenly brown.
For the gravy, cook onion and tomato until soft, blend, and strain.
Cook the gravy down for twelve minutes with garam masala and salt.
Add the cream if using, and thin with water to a spoonable consistency.
Add the koftas at the last minute so they stay whole.

name: Dum Aloo
steps: Boil the potatoes, peel them, and prick each one all over with a fork.
Fry them in oil until they wrinkle and turn gold, then lift them out.
Whisk the curd with the turmeric, red chilli powder and salt so it will not split.
Fry cumin and onion, add the tomato, then lower the heat and stir the curd in slowly.
Return the potatoes and simmer for ten minutes, covered, on the lowest flame.
Finish with garam masala.

name: Jeera Aloo
steps: Boil the potatoes until just done and cut into cubes — slightly undercooked is better than mushy.
Heat the oil and fry the cumin until it darkens and smells nutty.
Add the potatoes and turmeric and toss until every cube is yellow.
Press them down for a minute at a time to get crisp edges.
Season with red chilli powder and salt, and finish with lemon.

name: Karela Sabzi
steps: Scrape the ridges off the karela, slice into rounds and rub with salt. Leave fifteen minutes, then squeeze out the water — this takes most of the bitterness out.
Fry the cumin and onion in oil until golden.
Add the karela and turmeric and cook on a medium flame for twelve minutes, turning often.
Add the amchur and salt and cook two more minutes.
Serve with roti — the bitterness is the point, but the amchur balances it.

name: Arbi Masala
steps: Boil the arbi until a knife slides in, then peel and cut into thick rounds.
Let them dry completely — wet arbi spits in hot oil.
Fry the ajwain in oil, then the arbi, turning until the edges crisp.
Add the onion if using and cook until soft.
Stir in the turmeric, coriander powder, amchur and salt, and toss for two minutes.
Serve with dal and rice.

name: Parwal Sabzi
steps: Scrape the parwal lightly and cut into thick diagonal slices.
Fry the cumin in oil, then add the parwal and potato if using.
Add the turmeric, coriander powder and salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on a low flame for ten minutes — parwal releases its own water.
Add the tomato if using and cook uncovered for three minutes.
Serve as a side with dal.

name: Kadhi Pakora
steps: Beat half the besan with water into a thick batter, season with salt and chilli, and fry small spoonfuls in oil until golden. These are the pakoras.
Whisk the curd with the rest of the besan and a cup of water until completely smooth.
Cook the kadhi on a low flame for fifteen minutes, stirring, until it thickens. Never let it boil hard.
Pop mustard seeds in a little oil with the curry leaves and pour over.
Slide the pakoras in, add salt, and simmer for five minutes.
Serve over plain rice.

name: Soya Chunk Curry
steps: Soak the soya chunks in hot water for fifteen minutes, then squeeze them out hard — twice if you can, the water tastes of cardboard.
Brown the onion in oil until it is genuinely dark golden.
Add ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the masala thickens.
Add the chunks, turmeric, salt and a cup of water, and simmer ten minutes so they absorb the gravy.
Finish with garam masala and serve with rice.

name: Chicken Korma
steps: Soak the cashews in warm water, then grind to a smooth paste.
Fry the sliced onion slowly in oil until deep brown — take fifteen minutes over it.
Add the cardamom and cinnamon, then the chicken, and turn it until it loses its pink colour.
Lower the heat and stir in the whisked curd a spoon at a time so it does not split.
Add the cashew paste and salt, cover, and cook for twenty-five minutes.
Finish with garam masala and rest five minutes before serving.

name: Mutton Curry
steps: Fry the onion in oil for ten minutes until it is soft and sweet.
Add the ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the masala darkens.
Add the mutton and sear it in the masala for five minutes.
Stir in the curd if using, then turmeric, coriander powder and salt.
Pressure cook for twenty minutes, or cover and simmer for fifty, until the meat gives way.
Uncover, add the garam masala, and cook off the liquid until the gravy coats the meat.

name: Keema Matar
steps: Ask for the mutton minced fine, or pulse it in a blender in short bursts.
Fry the onion until golden, then add ginger and garlic.
Add the tomatoes and cook until they break down completely.
Add the mince and break it up with the spoon — no lumps, or it will not brown.
Cook for ten minutes, then add the peas, turmeric and salt with half a cup of water.
Simmer eight minutes, finish with garam masala, and serve with pav or roti.

name: Matar Mushroom
steps: Wipe the mushrooms and quarter them — washing them makes them waterlogged.
Sear them in a dry hot pan for three minutes until they squeak and brown, then set aside.
In the same pan, heat the oil, add cumin, garlic and onion, and fry until soft.
Add the tomato if using, then the peas with a splash of water, and cook five minutes.
Return the mushrooms, add turmeric and salt, and toss for two minutes.
Finish with garam masala.

name: Idli
steps: Bring the batter to room temperature and stir it gently — do not beat the air out of it.
Taste for salt; fermented batter often needs a pinch more than you think.
Grease the idli plates lightly and pour in the batter without filling to the brim.
Steam for twelve minutes. They are done when a knife comes out clean.
Rest for two minutes before unmoulding, and serve with chutney and sambar.

name: Masala Dosa
steps: Boil the potatoes, then crush them roughly rather than mashing to a paste.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves, chilli and onion, and fry until soft.
Add turmeric and salt, then the potatoes, and mix for two minutes. Keep it a little chunky.
Spread a ladle of batter on a hot tawa in a spiral, drizzle oil round the edge, and cook until the underside is lace-brown.
Spoon the filling along the middle, fold, and serve with coconut chutney.

name: Rava Dosa
steps: Mix the rava, maida, salt and cumin with the water into a batter as thin as milk.
Stir in the chopped onion, chilli and curry leaves, and rest for twenty minutes.
Get the tawa very hot and rub it with half an onion — this stops the dosa sticking.
Pour the batter from a height in a quick circle so it makes a lacy net rather than a solid disc.
Drizzle oil round the edge and cook until crisp, then fold. No flipping needed.

name: Onion Uttapam
steps: Chop the onion, tomato, carrot and chilli small and keep them separate from the batter.
Spread a thick ladle of batter on a medium-hot tawa — uttapam should be thicker than dosa.
Scatter the vegetables over the top and press them in gently with the back of the ladle.
Drizzle oil around the edge and cook for three minutes until the base sets.
Flip carefully and cook two more minutes, then serve with chutney.

name: Medu Vada
steps: Soak the urad dal and rice for three hours, then grind with very little water into a thick, fluffy batter.
The batter is right when a spoonful dropped in water floats. If it sinks, grind a little more.
Fold in the onion, chilli, curry leaves and salt.
Wet your palm, put a blob of batter on it, flatten and poke a hole through the middle.
Slide into medium-hot oil and fry until deep golden on both sides.
Drain and serve with sambar and chutney.

name: Coconut Chutney
steps: Grind the coconut with the chilli, ginger and salt, adding water a spoon at a time.
Stop while it is still slightly coarse — over-grinding turns it sweet and pasty.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds and add the curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the chutney and stir once.
Serve with idli or dosa.

name: Tomato Chutney
steps: Fry the onion and garlic in oil until soft and just coloured.
Add the tomatoes and chilli and cook for eight minutes until they collapse.
Cool slightly, then grind to a coarse chutney.
Return to the pan and cook off any extra water for two minutes.
Season and serve with dosa.

name: Vegetable Kurma
steps: Cut the vegetables into even pieces and boil them with turmeric and salt until just tender.
Grind the coconut with a little water into a thick paste.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add the onion and fry until golden.
Add the cooked vegetables with their water, then the coconut paste.
Simmer for eight minutes without boiling hard, and serve with dosa or rice.

name: Avial
steps: Cut every vegetable into batons roughly the same thickness so they cook together.
Boil them with turmeric and salt until just done — they should still bite back.
Grind the coconut with a splash of water to a coarse paste and stir it in.
Take the pan off the heat before adding the curd, or it will split.
Add the coconut milk if using, and a drizzle of raw oil on top.
Pop the mustard seeds in a little hot oil and pour over before serving.

name: Beans Thoran
steps: Top and tail the beans and slice them very fine — this is the whole dish.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves, chilli and onion, and fry until soft.
Add the beans, turmeric and salt, and toss over a high flame for two minutes.
Cover and cook for six minutes on a low flame with no water.
Uncover, add the coconut, and toss for a minute until the raw smell goes.

name: Beetroot Poriyal
steps: Peel and grate the beetroot — grating cooks faster and keeps the colour.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves and onion, and fry until soft.
Add the beetroot and salt and toss for two minutes.
Cover and cook on a low flame for seven minutes, stirring once so it does not catch.
Finish with coconut if you have it.

name: Chow Chow Kootu
steps: Boil the moong dal with turmeric and salt until soft but not mushy.
Peel and cube the chow chow and boil it separately until tender — it gives off a lot of water.
Grind the coconut with the cumin and a little water to a coarse paste.
Combine the dal, vegetable and coconut paste and simmer for five minutes.
Pop mustard seeds in oil and pour over.
Serve with rice.

name: Lemon Rasam
steps: Cook the toor dal with turmeric until soft and mash it.
Simmer the tomato in two cups of water for six minutes, then mash it into the water.
Add the dal, crushed pepper, cumin, rasam powder and salt.
Bring it to the edge of a boil and take it off the heat.
Squeeze in the lemon juice only now — heat makes it bitter.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves in oil and pour over.

name: Mor Kuzhambu
steps: Boil the cubed chow chow with turmeric and salt until tender, and let it cool slightly.
Grind the coconut with the green chilli and a little water to a smooth paste.
Whisk the curd with the besan so it will not split, then stir in the coconut paste.
Add the curd mixture to the vegetable on the lowest heat and warm it through — do not let it boil.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves in oil and pour over.
Serve with rice.

name: Puliyogare
steps: Cook the rice so the grains stay separate, then spread it out to cool.
Soak the tamarind in hot water and squeeze out the thick pulp.
Fry the peanuts in oil and set aside, then pop mustard seeds and add curry leaves and turmeric.
Pour in the tamarind pulp with the jaggery and salt and cook until it thickens and darkens — about eight minutes.
Fold the cooled rice through the tamarind mixture until it is evenly stained.
Top with the peanuts and rest for ten minutes before eating.

name: Coconut Rice
steps: Cook the rice and cool it completely — warm rice goes gluey when you fold coconut through it.
Fry the cashews in oil until pale gold and set aside.
Pop the mustard seeds, add curry leaves and chilli, then the grated coconut.
Fry the coconut for two minutes only, until it smells sweet but has not browned.
Fold the rice and salt through, add the cashews, and serve.

name: Curd Semiya
steps: Roast the vermicelli in a dry pan until it smells nutty, then boil it in salted water for four minutes and drain.
Run it under cold water so it stops cooking, then let it dry a little.
Whisk the curd with salt and a splash of water until pourable.
Fold the cooled vermicelli into the curd.
Temper mustard seeds, curry leaves and ginger in oil and pour over.

name: Semiya Upma
steps: Dry roast the vermicelli until it turns a shade darker, then set aside.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves, chilli and onion, and fry until soft.
Add the carrot and stir for a minute.
Pour in the water with salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Add the vermicelli, cover, and cook for three minutes until the water is absorbed.
Fluff with a fork and serve with a squeeze of lemon.

name: Rava Kesari
steps: Roast the rava in a tablespoon of ghee until it smells nutty and no longer looks raw.
Fry the cashews and raisins in more ghee and set aside.
Boil the water with the sugar and cardamom.
Add the roasted rava in a stream, stirring hard so no lumps form — it will spit.
Stir in the rest of the ghee, cover for two minutes, then top with the nuts.
Serve warm; it sets firm as it cools.

name: Semiya Payasam
steps: Fry the vermicelli in the ghee until golden — this keeps it from going sticky in the milk.
Bring the milk to a boil and simmer it for five minutes to reduce slightly.
Add the vermicelli and cook for eight minutes until soft.
Stir in the sugar and cardamom and cook three more minutes.
Fry the cashews and raisins in a little ghee and scatter over.
Serve warm or chilled; it thickens a lot as it stands.

name: Chicken Chettinad
steps: Dry roast the fennel and half the pepper, then grind with the coconut into a coarse masala.
Fry the curry leaves and onion in oil until the onion is deep brown.
Add the ginger, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the masala is thick.
Add the chicken and turmeric and turn it until it is coated and no longer pink.
Add the ground masala and salt with half a cup of water, cover, and cook for twenty minutes.
Crush the remaining pepper over the top and serve with rice or dosa.

name: Fish Moilee
steps: Rub the fish with turmeric and salt and leave it for ten minutes.
Fry the onion, ginger, chilli and curry leaves gently in oil — no browning, this curry stays pale.
Add the tomato if using and cook until it softens.
Pour in half the coconut milk with a cup of water and bring to a bare simmer.
Slide the fish in and cook for eight minutes without stirring, just shaking the pan.
Add the rest of the coconut milk, warm through, and take it off before it boils.

name: Prawn Masala
steps: Devein the prawns and rub them with turmeric and salt.
Fry the onion in oil until golden, then add ginger, garlic and curry leaves.
Add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a thick masala.
Add the prawns and cook for four minutes only — they turn rubbery fast.
Stir in the coconut if using and the red chilli powder, and serve immediately.

name: Potato Podimas
steps: Boil the potatoes, peel them, and crumble them with your fingers rather than mashing.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves, chilli and onion, and fry until soft.
Add turmeric and salt, then the potatoes.
Toss for four minutes until everything is yellow and hot through.
Finish with a squeeze of lemon.

name: Raw Banana Poriyal
steps: Peel the raw banana and cut it into cubes, dropping them straight into water with a pinch of turmeric so they do not blacken.
Boil the cubes in salted water for eight minutes until just tender, then drain.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add curry leaves and onion, and fry until soft.
Add the banana cubes and turmeric and toss gently — they break easily.
Finish with the coconut and a pinch of salt.

name: Begun Bhaja
steps: Cut the brinjal into thick rounds about half an inch across and soak them in salted water for ten minutes.
Pat them completely dry, then rub with turmeric, chilli powder and salt.
Dust each slice lightly with besan if using — it gives a crisper edge.
Shallow fry in hot oil for three minutes a side until deep brown.
Drain on paper and serve with dal and rice.

name: Aloo Phulkopir Torkari
steps: Cut the potatoes into wedges and the cauliflower into florets of a similar size.
Fry the cumin in oil, then the potatoes for three minutes.
Add the cauliflower and fry until the edges take on colour.
Add turmeric, salt, the sugar and the tomato if using, then half a cup of hot water.
Cover and cook for twelve minutes until both are tender and the water has almost gone.
Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil if you have it.

name: Cholar Dal
steps: Soak the chana dal for an hour, then boil it with turmeric and salt until soft but still whole. Do not overboil it into paste.
Fry the cumin and ginger in oil, then add the coconut and raisins and fry for a minute.
Pour the dal in with a little of its water.
Add the sugar and simmer for five minutes — Bengali dal is meant to be slightly sweet.
Serve with luchi or rice.

name: Bhaja Moong Dal
steps: Dry roast the moong dal in a pan until it turns pale gold and smells nutty — this is the whole character of the dish.
Rinse it, then boil with turmeric and salt until soft.
Fry cumin, ginger and chilli in oil for a minute.
Pour the dal in, add hot water to loosen it, and simmer for five minutes.
Serve with rice.

name: Doi Maach
steps: Rub the fish with turmeric and salt and fry it lightly in oil, one minute a side. Lift it out.
Whisk the curd smooth with the ginger, sugar and salt.
Fry the onion in the same oil until soft, then take the pan off the heat.
Stir the curd in off the heat so it cannot split, then return to a low flame.
Slide the fish back in and simmer for eight minutes, shaking the pan rather than stirring.
Serve with rice.

name: Chingri Malai Curry
steps: Rub the prawns with turmeric and salt, then fry them for one minute a side and set aside.
Make a paste of the onion, ginger and chilli.
Fry the paste in the oil until the raw smell goes and it turns pale gold.
Pour in the coconut milk with the sugar and salt and simmer gently for five minutes.
Return the prawns and warm them through for three minutes — no longer.
Serve with plain rice.

name: Mutton Kosha
steps: Fry the onion in oil for fifteen minutes until it is dark, sweet and almost jammy. This is the base.
Add the ginger and garlic and cook two more minutes.
Add the mutton and fry it hard in the masala for eight minutes.
Stir in the curd if using, then the turmeric, chilli powder, sugar and salt.
Cover and cook on a low flame for fifty minutes, adding a splash of water only if it starts to catch.
Add the fried potatoes if using in the last twenty minutes.
Finish with garam masala once the oil has separated.

name: Labra
steps: Chop every vegetable into pieces of roughly the same size — this dish is about even cooking.
Pop the mustard seeds and kalonji in oil, then add the vegetables and toss for three minutes.
Add turmeric and salt and stir to coat.
Cover and cook on a low flame for twenty minutes, shaking the pan instead of stirring.
Uncover and cook off any water until the vegetables are glazed.
Serve with rice or luchi.

name: Chirer Pulao
steps: Rinse the poha briefly in a colander and leave it to drain — do not soak it.
Fry the peanuts in oil and set aside, then fry the raisins for twenty seconds.
Add cumin, then the peas and carrot, and cook for three minutes.
Add the poha, turmeric, sugar and salt and fold gently.
Cover for two minutes to heat through, then top with the peanuts and raisins.

name: Payesh
steps: Rinse the rice and soak it for twenty minutes — this helps it break down into the milk.
Bring the milk to a boil and simmer for ten minutes, stirring so it does not catch.
Add the drained rice and cook on a low flame for twenty minutes, stirring often.
Add the sugar and cardamom and cook another five minutes. The rice should be barely visible.
Fry the cashews and raisins in ghee and stir through.
Serve warm, or cold the way it is often eaten the next day.

name: Shrikhand
steps: Hang the curd in a muslin cloth over a bowl for four hours, or overnight in the fridge, until it stops dripping.
You should be left with about half the volume — that is the chakka.
Warm the milk and steep the saffron in it for five minutes.
Beat the chakka with the sugar until it is completely smooth and grain-free.
Stir in the cardamom and saffron milk, and top with slivered almonds.
Chill before serving.

name: Gujarati Dal
steps: Boil the toor dal with turmeric and salt until completely soft, then mash it.
Add the jaggery and tomato if using and simmer for five minutes.
The dal should taste sweet, sour and salty all at once — adjust with more jaggery if it is flat.
Pop mustard seeds and cumin in oil, add the curry leaves and peanuts, and fry for a minute.
Pour the tempering in and serve with rice.

name: Vagharelo Bhaat
steps: Rinse and soak the rice for fifteen minutes, then drain.
Fry the cumin, cinnamon and cloves in oil until they smell warm.
Add the peas, carrot and tomato and cook for two minutes.
Add the rice, turmeric and salt and stir for a minute.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for twelve minutes.
Rest five minutes and fork through.

name: Bataka Nu Shaak
steps: Cut the potatoes into cubes and the tomatoes into wedges.
Pop the mustard seeds in oil, then add the potatoes and fry for three minutes.
Add turmeric, coriander powder, sugar and salt and toss to coat.
Add the tomatoes and half a cup of water, cover, and cook for twelve minutes.
Mash a couple of potato cubes to thicken the gravy and serve with rotli.

name: Methi Thepla
steps: Chop the methi very fine and knead it into the atta with the curd, spices, salt and a spoon of oil.
The dough should be firm — softer than chapati dough, or the theplas will not keep.
Rest for ten minutes, then roll into thin discs.
Cook on a hot tawa, turning twice and brushing with oil, until brown spots appear.
Stack them under a cloth. They keep for two days in a box, which is the point.

name: Muthiya
steps: Grate the lauki and squeeze out most of the water — keep a few spoons of it for the dough.
Mix the atta, besan, lauki, methi, turmeric and salt into a stiff dough with that reserved water.
Roll into thick cylinders and steam for twenty minutes.
Cool, then slice into thick coins.
Pop mustard seeds and sesame in oil and toss the slices until they are crisp at the edges.
Serve with green chutney or tea.

name: Handvo
steps: Mix the rava, besan, curd, sugar and salt with water into a thick batter and leave it for two hours to soften.
Grate the lauki and squeeze out the water, then fold it into the batter.
Heat a heavy pan with a generous layer of oil and pop the mustard seeds.
Pour the batter in, scatter sesame on top, cover, and cook on a low flame for fifteen minutes.
Flip carefully and cook the other side for ten minutes.
Cut into wedges and serve hot.

name: Misal Pav
steps: Sprout the beans a day ahead, or use ready sprouts. Boil them with turmeric and salt until tender.
Fry cumin, garlic and half the onion until golden, then add the tomatoes and cook down hard.
Add the coriander powder and red chilli powder and cook until the oil floats.
Add the sprouts with a cup of water and simmer for fifteen minutes. The gravy, the 'kat', should be thin and fiery.
Top with the remaining raw onion and a spoon of coconut if you have it.
Serve with the bread, which is there to mop, not to be eaten separately.

name: Kanda Poha
steps: Rinse the poha in a colander under running water for thirty seconds and leave it to drain.
Fry the peanuts in oil and set aside, then pop the mustard seeds and add the onion and potato.
Cook until the onion is soft and the potato is done, about six minutes.
Add turmeric, sugar and salt, then fold the poha in gently.
Cover for two minutes, then finish with lemon, coriander and the peanuts.

name: Sabudana Khichdi
steps: Rinse the sabudana twice and soak it in just enough water to cover for four hours. Each pearl should be soft but separate — wet sabudana turns to glue.
Drain it well and mix in the salt.
Roast the peanuts, rub off the skins and crush them coarsely.
Fry cumin in oil, add the potato cubes and cook until done.
Add the sabudana and peanuts and stir gently over a low flame for four minutes.
Finish with lemon and coriander, and eat straight away.

name: Thalipeeth
steps: Mix the three flours with the chopped onion, coriander, cumin, turmeric and salt.
Add water a spoon at a time and knead into a soft dough that just holds together.
Pat a ball flat on a greased sheet of paper with wet fingers, until it is about a quarter inch thick.
Make a small hole in the middle so it cooks evenly.
Transfer to a hot tawa, drizzle oil into the hole and around the edge, and cook for three minutes a side.
Serve with curd or butter.

name: Pithla
steps: Whisk the besan with the water until there are no lumps at all — this is the whole trick.
Pop mustard seeds in oil, add the onion, chilli and garlic, and fry until golden.
Add turmeric and salt, then pour the besan slurry in slowly while stirring.
Cook on a low flame for eight minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens and turns glossy.
It should be pourable, not stiff — add hot water if it tightens.
Finish with coriander and serve with bhakri or rice.

name: Zunka
steps: Fry mustard seeds, garlic, chilli and onion in oil until the onion is properly golden.
Add turmeric and salt, then sprinkle the dry besan over the top.
Stir constantly over a low flame — the besan will clump, and you want small clumps, not big ones.
Cook for eight minutes until it smells toasted and looks like coarse crumbs.
Scatter coriander and serve with bhakri and a spoon of ghee.

name: Varan Bhaat
steps: Cook the toor dal with turmeric and salt until soft, then mash it smooth.
Cook the rice separately so the grains stay separate.
Loosen the dal with hot water until it pours — varan is meant to be thin.
Fry the cumin in ghee for thirty seconds and pour it into the dal.
Serve the dal over the rice with more ghee on top and a squeeze of lemon.

name: Kothimbir Vadi
steps: Chop the coriander finely — a whole bunch, stems and all.
Mix the besan, coriander, chilli, turmeric and salt with water into a thick batter.
Pour into a greased tin and steam for twenty minutes until set.
Cool completely, then cut into thick fingers.
Pop mustard seeds and sesame in oil and fry the pieces until crisp on both sides.
Serve with chutney.

name: Veg Manchurian
steps: Shred the cabbage and grate the carrot, then squeeze the mixture in your fist to get the water out.
Mix with the cornflour, maida and salt into a stiff mixture that holds when pressed.
Roll into small balls and deep fry in medium-hot oil until golden. If they break up, add more cornflour.
For the sauce, fry the garlic and spring onion in a spoon of oil, then add the soy sauce, vinegar and half a cup of water.
Thicken with a slurry of cornflour and water, then toss the balls through it just before serving so they stay crisp.

name: Gobi Manchurian
steps: Break the cauliflower into small florets and blanch them in salted water for three minutes, then drain and dry.
Make a thick batter with the cornflour, maida, salt, pepper and water.
Coat the florets and deep fry until crisp and golden.
Fry the garlic and spring onion in a spoon of oil, add the soy sauce, ketchup and a splash of water.
Toss the fried florets through the sauce over a high flame for a minute and serve immediately.

name: Chilli Paneer
steps: Cube the paneer and toss it in the cornflour with a pinch of salt.
Fry the paneer in hot oil until the edges crisp, then lift it out.
In the same pan, stir-fry the garlic, onion and capsicum on a high flame for two minutes — keep them crunchy.
Add the soy sauce, ketchup, vinegar and a splash of water and let it bubble.
Return the paneer, toss to coat, and serve at once.

name: Chilli Chicken
steps: Cut the chicken into small even pieces and toss with the cornflour, soy sauce and salt.
Leave it for fifteen minutes, then fry in hot oil until browned and just cooked.
Stir-fry the garlic, onion, capsicum and green chilli on a high flame for two minutes.
Add the vinegar, the rest of the soy sauce and a little water, and bring to a bubble.
Return the chicken, toss for a minute so it glazes, and serve with fried rice.

name: Veg Hakka Noodles
steps: Boil the noodles a minute short of the packet time, drain, and rinse under cold water with a drop of oil.
Slice the vegetables into thin matchsticks so they cook in seconds.
Get the pan very hot, add the oil and garlic, then the vegetables, and stir-fry for two minutes.
Add the noodles, soy sauce, salt and pepper, and toss with two spoons rather than stirring.
Finish with spring onion and serve straight away.

name: Schezwan Noodles
steps: Boil and drain the noodles, then toss them with a little oil so they do not clump.
Make a quick schezwan base: fry the chopped garlic in oil, add the red chilli powder, ketchup and vinegar and cook for a minute.
Add the capsicum and carrot and stir-fry on a high flame for two minutes.
Add the noodles, soy sauce and salt and toss until evenly red.
Top with spring onion and serve hot.

name: Chilli Garlic Fried Rice
steps: Use rice cooked the day before, broken up with your fingers.
Chop the garlic fine and fry it in hot oil until it is just turning gold — burnt garlic ruins the dish.
Add the white parts of the spring onion and the carrot and stir-fry for a minute.
Add the rice and toss over a high flame, then splash the soy sauce around the rim of the pan.
Season with pepper and salt, add the green tops of the spring onion, and serve.

name: Honey Chilli Potato
steps: Cut the potatoes into thick fries and parboil them for four minutes, then drain and dry completely.
Toss with the cornflour and salt and deep fry until crisp and golden.
In a wide pan, fry the garlic in a spoon of oil, then add the honey, soy sauce and red chilli powder.
Let the sauce bubble until it thickens and looks syrupy.
Toss the fries through it off the heat so they stay crisp, and top with sesame and spring onion.

name: Sweet Corn Soup
steps: Blitz half the corn with a cup of water into a rough purée and keep the rest whole.
Warm the oil, add the garlic, then the purée and three cups of water, and bring to a simmer.
Add the whole corn and the diced carrot and cook for eight minutes.
Mix the cornflour with cold water and stir it in to thicken, then simmer two more minutes.
Season with salt and plenty of pepper, and finish with spring onion.

name: Hot and Sour Soup
steps: Shred the cabbage and cut the carrot and mushroom into thin strips.
Fry the garlic in the oil for thirty seconds, then add the vegetables and stir-fry for two minutes.
Add four cups of water and the soy sauce and simmer for eight minutes.
Thicken with cornflour mixed with cold water, stirring as it goes in.
Take it off the heat and add the vinegar — adding it earlier cooks the sourness away.
Season hard with black pepper and serve.

name: Garlic Bread
steps: Mash the butter with finely grated garlic, salt and chopped coriander.
Slice the bread thickly, not all the way through, and spread the butter into the cuts.
Wrap in foil and bake at 200°C for eight minutes.
Open the foil, add the cheese if using, and bake five more minutes until the top is golden.

name: Creamy Mushroom Pasta
steps: Boil the pasta in well-salted water and keep a mug of the cooking water before draining.
Sear the sliced mushrooms in a dry hot pan until they squeak and brown, then add the oil, butter and garlic.
Pour in the cream and let it bubble for two minutes.
Add the pasta and toss, loosening with the cooking water until the sauce coats every piece.
Season with pepper and salt, and grate the cheese over the top.

name: Tomato Bruschetta
steps: Dice the tomatoes and toss with salt, pepper, the olive oil and chopped herbs. Leave for ten minutes so they release their juice.
Toast the bread until crisp and rub a cut garlic clove across each slice while it is still hot.
Spoon the tomatoes on just before serving, and pour a little of the juices over.
Eat straight away, before the bread softens.

name: Baked Potato Wedges
steps: Cut the potatoes into wedges, skin on, and soak them in cold water for ten minutes to rinse off the starch.
Dry them thoroughly with a cloth — wet wedges steam instead of crisping.
Toss with the oil, salt, pepper and chilli powder.
Spread on a tray in a single layer with space between them and bake at 220°C for twenty minutes.
Turn once halfway. Serve with ketchup or a dip.

name: Coleslaw
steps: Shred the cabbage as finely as you can and grate the carrot.
Sprinkle with salt and leave for ten minutes, then squeeze out the water that comes off.
Fold through the mayonnaise, lemon juice and pepper.
Chill for twenty minutes before serving — it improves.

name: French Toast
steps: Beat the eggs with the milk, sugar and a pinch of cardamom until no streaks remain.
Soak each slice of bread for twenty seconds a side — enough to drink the custard without falling apart.
Melt the butter in a pan on a medium flame.
Fry each slice for two minutes a side until golden and set in the middle.
Serve hot with honey or jam.

name: Eggless Pancakes
steps: Whisk the maida, sugar, baking powder and salt together.
Add the milk gradually to a smooth batter, then rest it for ten minutes.
Heat a non-stick pan on a medium flame and wipe it with a little butter.
Pour a ladleful and wait for bubbles to appear across the surface before flipping.
Cook one more minute on the other side and stack them under a cloth.

name: Grilled Cheese Sandwich
steps: Butter the outside of each slice, not the inside — that is what makes it crisp.
Layer the cheese and thin tomato slices between two slices, and grind pepper over the cheese.
Cook in a pan on a low-to-medium flame, pressing gently with a spatula.
Three minutes a side, until the outside is golden and the cheese has given way.
Cut on the diagonal and eat while the cheese still pulls.

name: Mango Lassi
steps: Peel and chop the mango, keeping a few cubes back for the top.
Blend the rest with the curd, sugar and cardamom until completely smooth.
Thin with milk if it is too thick to drink through a straw.
Chill and serve with the reserved mango cubes on top.

name: Banana Smoothie
steps: The riper and more speckled the bananas, the sweeter the smoothie — no sugar needed.
Break them into the blender with the milk, curd and cardamom.
Blend until there are no lumps at all.
Taste, add honey only if it needs it, and pour over ice.

name: Nimbu Pani
steps: Squeeze the lemons and strain out the pips.
Stir the sugar into a little warm water until it dissolves, then top with cold water.
Add the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and the crushed mint.
Taste — it should be sharp, sweet and just slightly salty all at once.
Serve over plenty of ice.

name: Gajar Halwa
steps: Grate the carrots — the fine side of the grater, not the coarse one.
Cook them with the milk on a low flame for twenty minutes, stirring now and then, until the milk is nearly gone.
Add the sugar and keep stirring; the mixture will loosen again as the sugar melts.
Add the ghee and cook until it starts to leave the sides of the pan.
Stir in the khoya if using and the cardamom.
Top with cashews fried in a little ghee.

name: Suji Halwa
steps: Roast the rava in half the ghee on a low flame until it is golden and smells nutty — this takes a good eight minutes, do not rush it.
Fry the cashews and raisins in a little more ghee and set aside.
Boil the water with the sugar and cardamom in a separate pan.
Pour the boiling syrup into the rava carefully — it will bubble violently.
Stir hard until it thickens and pulls away from the pan.
Stir in the rest of the ghee and the nuts, and serve hot.

name: Besan Ladoo
steps: Melt the ghee in a heavy pan and add the besan.
Roast on the lowest flame for fifteen minutes, stirring without stopping. It should turn a deep gold and smell like toasted nuts — under-roasted besan tastes raw.
Take it off the heat and let it cool for ten minutes until you can touch it.
Stir in the sugar and cardamom, and chopped almonds if using.
Roll into balls while still warm; if it crumbles, add a spoon of warm ghee.
Cool completely before storing.

name: Rice Kheer
steps: Rinse and soak the rice for half an hour, then drain.
Bring the milk to a boil and simmer for ten minutes, stirring so it does not catch.
Add the rice and cook on a low flame for twenty-five minutes, stirring often.
Add the sugar and cardamom and cook five more minutes.
Steep the saffron in a spoon of warm milk and stir it in.
Top with fried cashews and raisins, and serve warm or cold.

name: Chocolate Cake
steps: Beat the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy — a good five minutes, and do not shortcut it.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each, then the vanilla.
Sift the maida, cocoa, baking powder and salt together and fold in alternately with the milk.
Pour into a lined tin and bake at 180°C for thirty-five minutes.
A skewer in the middle should come out with a crumb or two, not wet batter.
Cool in the tin for ten minutes before turning out.

name: Butter Cookies
steps: Beat the soft butter and sugar for four minutes until light.
Add the vanilla, then the maida, baking powder and salt, and bring it together into a soft dough.
Do not knead — the more you work it, the tougher the biscuit.
Roll into a log, chill for twenty minutes, then slice into coins.
Bake at 170°C for twelve minutes until the edges are just gold.
Cool on the tray for five minutes before moving them.

name: Coconut Ladoo
steps: Warm the condensed milk gently in a heavy pan.
Add the grated coconut and the cardamom and stir for eight minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides.
It should hold together when pressed — if it is still loose, keep going.
Let it cool until you can handle it, then roll into small balls.
Roll each in a little dry coconut and leave to firm up.

name: Masala Oats
steps: Fry the cumin in oil, then add the onion, chilli and carrot and cook until soft.
Add the tomato, turmeric and salt and cook until it collapses.
Add the oats and stir for a minute so they take on the masala.
Pour in the water and simmer for four minutes, stirring, until it is thick and porridge-like.
Eat straight away — oats set solid if they sit.

name: Broccoli Stir-fry
steps: Cut the broccoli into small florets and blanch in salted boiling water for two minutes, then drain hard.
Get the pan smoking hot and add the mustard oil — it should shimmer.
Add the garlic and stir for fifteen seconds, then the broccoli and capsicum.
Stir-fry for three minutes without moving it too much, so it chars in spots.
Splash the soy sauce around the edge, season with pepper, and serve at once.

name: Zucchini Sabzi
steps: Cut the zucchini into thick half-moons — thin slices turn to mush.
Fry cumin in oil, then the onion until soft and golden.
Add the zucchini and turmeric and toss for two minutes.
Add the salt and coriander powder, cover, and cook for six minutes on a low flame.
Uncover, add the tomato if using, and cook off the water for three minutes.

name: Sweet Potato Chaat
steps: Boil the sweet potatoes whole until a knife slides through, then peel and cube them.
Let them cool a little — hot cubes fall apart when you toss them.
Toss with the lemon juice, chaat masala, salt and pepper.
Add the chopped onion and coriander and fold gently.
Serve warm as a snack or as a side with dal.

name: Pumpkin Sabzi
steps: Peel the pumpkin, discard the seeds, and cube the flesh.
Fry the kalonji in oil, add the onion and chilli, and cook until soft.
Add the pumpkin, turmeric and salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on a low flame for ten minutes — pumpkin releases plenty of water.
Uncover, add the jaggery if using, and cook off the liquid until glossy.

name: Tinda Sabzi
steps: Peel the tinda, cut into wedges and remove any hard seeds.
Fry cumin in oil, then the onion until golden, then the tomato until it breaks down.
Add the tinda, turmeric, coriander powder and salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on a low flame for twelve minutes, shaking the pan now and then.
Uncover and cook off the water until the masala clings to the pieces.

name: Shalgam Sabzi
steps: Peel the turnip and cut it into thick fingers — it shrinks a lot as it cooks.
Fry the cumin in oil, then the potato for three minutes so it starts to colour.
Add the turnip and fry for another three minutes.
Add the tomato, turmeric, coriander powder and salt with a splash of water.
Cover and cook for fifteen minutes until both vegetables are tender and the masala is thick.

name: Masala Chaas
steps: Toast the cumin in a dry pan and crush it.
Whisk the buttermilk with the salt, cumin and pepper.
Crush the curry leaves and coriander with your fingers and stir them in — crushing releases the flavour.
Chill and serve over ice.

name: Pav Bhaji
steps: Boil the potato, peas and carrot until soft, then mash roughly.
Fry half the onion in butter until golden, add the tomatoes and cook down hard.
Add the capsicum and cook for three minutes so it keeps some bite.
Add the mashed vegetables and the pav bhaji masala with a cup of water.
Mash everything together in the pan for ten minutes — bhaji is meant to be a rough mash, not a purée.
Finish with a knob of raw butter, and serve with the bread fried lightly in butter with the rest of the onion raw on the side.

name: Vegetable Biryani
steps: Soak the rice for twenty minutes and drain. Parboil it in salted water with the bay leaf and star anise until it is seventy per cent done, then drain.
Fry the sliced onion in oil until dark and crisp, and set half aside for the top.
Mix the curd with the biryani masala and salt, then fold the vegetables through it.
Layer the vegetables and rice in a heavy pot, scattering mint and the reserved onion between the layers.
Steep the saffron in warm milk and dribble it over the top.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest flame for twenty minutes, then rest for ten before opening.

name: Fruit Chaat
steps: Cut the apple and pineapple into small cubes and segment the orange.
Add the pomegranate seeds and sliced banana if using — add banana last so it does not brown.
Squeeze the lemon over and toss gently.
Dust with chaat masala and a pinch of salt, and serve straight away.

name: Penne Arrabbiata
steps: Boil the pasta in well-salted water and keep a mug of the water before draining.
Warm the olive oil gently and add the sliced garlic — it should soften and smell sweet, not brown.
Add the red chilli powder, then the tomato purée, and simmer for twelve minutes until it darkens.
Season with salt, and loosen with pasta water until it coats a spoon.
Toss the pasta through the sauce and finish with herbs.

name: Everyday Green Salad
steps: Wash the leaves and dry them properly — dressing slides off wet leaves.
Tear rather than cut the lettuce, and slice the cucumber and tomato.
Whisk the lemon juice with the olive oil, salt and pepper.
Dress the salad just before serving and toss with your hands.
